doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Kenny Burrell hires him after college
summary: He gives Kenny Burrell a tape as composer and arranger and is offered a gig, his first major job, in Detroit.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: And then every time, because it was like a Brazilian tune, right. So I go back to school, so every time like a Latin guest, or a person from like Puerto Rico or Brazil or something, every time they introduced a guest like that, I remember Catarina Valente was one of the guests [scats] that’s my tune. So I was like grinning you know. So going back again, Dr. Taylor and Leroy Kirkland and the next person that had an effect on me was Kenny Burrell. Because through Leroy Kirkland I met Kenny and I had given him a tape. And this was right after I got out of college. And I gave him this tape, of course it was a reel to reel, no cassettes them, big reel to reel, seven inch tape, all from college. Stuff that you played on. So I gave it to Kenny, it was on a Thursday night, Kenny said, “Okay, I’ll give it to you on Monday.” So I come home and my mother says, “You got a call from Kenny Burrell.” This was Friday. I said, “Really?” “Yeah, he said call him back.” So I said okay, so I’m in my mother’s room sitting at the table, I could see it right now. I picked the phone up, I called, I said, “Kenny, this is Allan Gumbs.” “You want a gig?” “What?” So, because I gave him a tape just as a composer and arranger. Because for some reason as much piano as I played, I never felt confident as a pianist.

I felt that somehow I wasn’t up to snuff to be considered to be able to do that. As much as I played, as much as I enjoyed it, I just felt that I didn’t have all that it takes to really be © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

in there. But he felt different. And I did my first major gig with Kenny Burrell in Detroit, at Baker’s Keyboard Lounge. And from there I met Earl Klugh. And we became friends, and another saxophone player who still lives in the Detroit area, his name is Allan Burns, a tenor player. So I was started to get slowly acclimated into this whole professional situation.
